metadata.title: Chapter 1: Numbers and Numeration
metadata.subject: Maths
learning_outcomes: Read and write 4-digit numbers up to 9999
Understand place value and face value of digits in a 4-digit number
Compare and order 4-digit numbers using symbols
Form greatest and smallest numbers from a given set of digits

ai_context.learning_goal: Mastery of 4-digit numbers, place value systems, and number comparison.
common_misconceptions: Confusing place value with face value.
Forgetting to include zeros when writing numbers in expanded form.

blocks.title: The Mystery of the Grand Library
blocks.body: Imagine walking into a magical, ancient library with shelves stretching up to the starry sky. There are exactly 999 books on the bottom floor, but today, a truck arrives with 1 brand new, heavy book. The librarian gasps—how do we count beyond 999? Where do we put the extra digit? Suddenly, a glowing golden box appears, creating a brand new column called 'Thousands'! Welcome to the wonderful world of large numbers, where counting never stops and every digit tells an exciting story about its value and position.

blocks.question: What comes right after the number 999?
blocks.explanation: When we add 1 to 999, we get 1000, which is our very first 4-digit number!

blocks.title: Concept 1: Entering the World of 4-Digit Numbers
blocks.body: Up until now, you have mastered numbers up to 999, which only have three columns: Ones, Tens, and Hundreds. But what happens when we add 1 to 999? We step into the realm of 4-digit numbers! A 4-digit number is made of Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, and Ones. For example, the number 4,382 is read as 'Four thousand three hundred eighty-two'. Every digit in this number has a specific home. The '4' lives in the Thousands house, the '3' in the Hundreds house, the '8' in the Tens house, and the '2' in the Ones house. Understanding this structure allows us to read and write any number up to 9,999 effortlessly.

blocks.title: Reading Numbers Aloud
blocks.front: How do you read the 4-digit number 7,054 in words?
blocks.back: Seven thousand fifty-four (Notice we skip reading the hundreds place since it is zero!).

blocks.title: The Comma Rule
blocks.body: When writing 4-digit numbers in standard mathematical form, we always place a comma after the thousands digit to make reading easier. For example: 5,432 instead of 5432. Think of the comma as a tiny breath you take when speaking the number aloud!

blocks.title: Concept 2: The Magic of Place Value
blocks.body: In mathematics, location is everything! The exact same digit can have completely different values depending on where it sits. This is known as [DICT_GRADE_TERM|place_value]. Let's take the number 5,555. The digit '5' appears four times, but each one has a different job! The first '5' on the left represents 5 thousands (5,000). The next '5' represents 5 hundreds (500). The third '5' represents 5 tens (50). The last '5' represents 5 ones (5). Contrast this with [DICT_GRADE_TERM|face_value], which is simply the digit's own true identity, regardless of where it lives. The face value of '5' is always just 5!

blocks.question: In the number 6,428, what is the place value of the digit 4?
blocks.explanation: The digit 4 is in the hundreds place, so its place value is 400.

blocks.title: Place Value vs Face Value
blocks.front: What is the difference between Place Value and Face Value?
blocks.back: Face value is the digit's actual value itself. Place value is the value of the digit based on its position in the number.

blocks.title: Concept 3: Expanding Numbers (Expanded Form)
blocks.body: Have you ever taken apart a toy robot to see all its individual gears and springs? We can do the exact same thing with numbers! Breaking a number apart to show the value of each digit is called writing it in [DICT_GRADE_TERM|expanded_form]. Let's take the number 3,425. When we stretch it out based on the place value of each digit, we get: 3,000 + 400 + 20 + 5. This tells us clearly that 3,425 is made by adding thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones together. It is like opening a treasure chest and counting every coin by its denomination!

blocks.question: Which of the following is the correct expanded form of 8,032?
blocks.explanation: 8 is in the thousands (8000), 3 is in the tens (30), and 2 is in the ones (2). The hundreds place has a zero, so it is skipped.

blocks.title: The Zero Trap in Expanded Form
blocks.body: Students often make mistakes when there is a zero in a number, like in 4,050. Remind yourself: zeros do not need to be written in expanded form because they hold no value in that position. 4,050 is simply 4,000 + 50!

blocks.title: Concept 4: Comparing Numbers (Who is Bigger?)
blocks.body: When two numbers meet in the jungle of mathematics, how do we know which one is larger? We use special alligator symbols: '>' (greater than), '<' (less than), and '=' (equal to). The alligator's mouth ALWAYS opens toward the larger number because it is extra hungry! To compare two 4-digit numbers, we follow a strict detective rule: Always start comparing from the highest place value on the left—the Thousands place! If the thousands are equal, move one step to the right and compare the Hundreds. If those are equal, check the Tens, and finally the Ones.

blocks.question: Which comparison statement is correct?
blocks.explanation: Comparing the tens place, 1 ten is less than 5 tens, so 4,215 is less than 4,251.

blocks.title: Alligator Mouth Rule
blocks.back: Greater than! The open mouth faces the bigger number.

blocks.title: Concept 5: Ordering Numbers (Ascending and Descending)
blocks.body: Numbers love to form neat lines! When we arrange numbers from the smallest to the largest, we call it [DICT_GRADE_TERM|ascending_order] (like climbing up a flight of stairs). When we arrange them from the largest to the smallest, we call it [DICT_GRADE_TERM|descending_order] (like walking down a slide or mountain). To order a group of 4-digit numbers, look at all their thousands first, sort them out, and then carefully compare their remaining digits to find their exact rank in the queue.

blocks.question: Arrange these numbers in ascending order: 3,402, 3,042, 3,420
blocks.explanation: Ascending means smallest to largest. 3,042 is smallest, followed by 3,402, and 3,420 is the largest.

blocks.title: Staircase Visualization
blocks.body: Draw a small staircase on your rough notebook when doing ordering problems. Label the bottom step 1 (smallest) and the top step 10 (largest) to never mix up ascending and descending order again!

blocks.title: Concept 6: Successor and Predecessor
blocks.body: Every number has neighbors! The number that comes immediately after a given number is called its [DICT_GRADE_TERM|successor]. To find the successor, we simply add 1 (+1) to the number. For example, the successor of 4,599 is 4,600. On the flip side, the number that comes immediately before a given number is called its [DICT_GRADE_TERM|predecessor]. To find the predecessor, we subtract 1 (-1) from the number. For example, the predecessor of 5,000 is 4,999. Neighbors are always just one step away!

blocks.question: What is the predecessor of 7,000?
blocks.explanation: Predecessor means the number right before. Subtracting 1 from 7,000 gives 6,999.

blocks.title: Successor Rule
blocks.front: How do you calculate the successor of any number?

blocks.title: Concept 7: Building Numbers (Greatest and Smallest)
blocks.body:
Suppose you are given a set of four distinct digits, such as 4, 1, 8, and 3, and asked to build the greatest and smallest possible 4-digit numbers. How do you do it like a master mathematician? To build the **greatest number**, arrange the digits in descending order from left to right (largest to smallest): 8,431. To build the **smallest number**, arrange the digits in ascending order from left to right (smallest to largest): 1,348. 

*Special Master Rule:* What if one of your digits is a 0, like 5, 0, 2, 9? You can never start a standard 4-digit number with 0 (because 0259 is just a 3-digit number, 259!). Instead, put the smallest non-zero digit first, place the 0 right in the second spot, and then arrange the rest normally: 2,059!

blocks.question: Using the digits 3, 0, 7, 5, what is the smallest possible 4-digit number you can form?
blocks.explanation: We cannot put 0 first. The next smallest digit is 3, followed immediately by 0, then 5 and 7, giving 3,057.

blocks.title: The Zero Trap in Number Building
blocks.body: Remind students: Zero is shy and hates standing at the very front of a 4-digit number line. Always give the second-smallest digit the front seat when zero is in your card deck!

blocks.title: Concept 8: Even and Odd Numbers
blocks.body: Numbers can also be sorted into two personality groups: Even and Odd! An [DICT_GRADE_TERM|even_number] is a number that can be divided into pairs with absolutely nothing left over. Even numbers always end in the digits 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. An [DICT_GRADE_TERM|odd_number] always leaves one leftover item when paired up, and they end in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9. Think of shoes in a shoe rack: even numbers match perfectly as pairs, while odd numbers always have one lone shoe looking for its partner!

blocks.question: Is the number 4,837 even or odd?
blocks.explanation: Look at the last digit (ones place). Since 7 is an odd digit, the entire number 4,837 is odd.

blocks.title: Even Number Endings
blocks.front: What digits do all even numbers end with?

blocks.title: Chapter Summary & Mastery Review
blocks.body: Congratulations on journeying through Chapter 1! You have unlocked the secrets of 4-digit numbers, conquered place value and face value, learned how to stretch numbers apart into expanded form, compared numbers using hungry alligator symbols, ordered numbers up and down staircases, found magical neighbors with successors and predecessors, built custom numbers from scratch, and even discovered the secret lives of even and odd numbers. You are now fully equipped to tackle any number challenge that comes your way!

blocks.question: What is the place value of 9 in the number 9,412?
blocks.explanation: The digit 9 is in the thousands place, so its place value is 9,000.
